ch1-q1.answer: Operations management manages the design and operation of processes that produce goods and services. A supply chain links raw-material suppliers to the final customer.
distractors: Operations management handles sales promotion only, while a supply chain handles internal payroll only.
Both operations management and a supply chain mean only advertising finished products.
Operations management handles financing only, while a supply chain covers only in-store work procedures.

ch1-q2.answer: Operations, Marketing, and Finance. Marketing identifies demand, Operations provides supply, and Finance secures funds.
distractors: Operations, Marketing, and Finance handle financing, production, and demand identification, respectively.
Operations, Marketing, and Finance work independently without exchanging information.
All three functions handle only selling; none deals with funds or supply.

ch1-q3.answer: The operations function transforms inputs into goods and services. Managers make decisions about capacity, processes, quality, inventory, and scheduling.
distractors: The operations function only advertises finished products, and its managers only choose advertising media.
The operations function only raises funds, and its managers do not deal with quality or scheduling.
The operations function records inputs but does not transform them into goods or services.

ch1-q4.answer: Differences include tangibility, storability, customer contact, quality measurement, and simultaneous production and consumption. Similarities include managing inputs, transformation, outputs, quality, capacity, schedules, and customer satisfaction.
distractors: Services can always be stored, while goods must always be produced and consumed simultaneously.
Only the need for quality management differs; goods production does not need it.
Goods and services do not share an input-transformation-output framework.

ch1-q5.answer: The Industrial Revolution brought mechanization and factories. Scientific management analyzes work scientifically. Interchangeable parts are standardized, replaceable components. Division of labor specializes work.
distractors: Scientific management relies on intuition, interchangeable parts are unique components, and division of labor means everyone does every task.
The Industrial Revolution returned production to handwork, and scientific management avoids observation and measurement.
Interchangeable parts mean specialized tasks, while division of labor means using standardized replacement components.

ch1-q6.answer: Services support employment and daily life. Manufacturing supplies tangible goods and supports other industries. Nonmanufactured goods include agricultural products and minerals.
distractors: Only services support daily life; manufacturing and agricultural goods have no connection to other industries.
Nonmanufactured goods include only cars and appliances assembled in factories.
Only manufacturing creates employment; services are not part of economic activity.

ch1-q7.answer: A model is a simplified representation of reality. Physical, schematic, and mathematical models support analysis and decision-making.
distractors: A model must reproduce every detail of reality without simplification to be useful.
Models are physical objects only; diagrams and equations are not models.
Models avoid simplifying reality and are not used for decision-making.

ch1-q8.answer: More customization requires greater process flexibility and skills, and changes how easily processes can be standardized or automated.
distractors: The degree of customization does not affect required skills or process flexibility.
More unique specifications always make automation with a single uniform process easier.
Customization affects only advertising and should not be considered in process planning.

ch1-q9.answer: Consider freedom versus cost for a car or public transport; immediate use versus future performance for buying a computer now or waiting; price versus reliability for new or used cars; initiative versus risk of error for speaking up; and reach, cost, and target customers for websites or newspaper ads.
distractors: Every alternative has identical costs and benefits, so no sacrifice is involved.
New cars are always cheaper than used cars, and waiting to buy still permits immediate use.
Public transport always offers more freedom than a car, and newspaper advertising is best for every customer group.

ch1-q10.answer: Craft production uses low volumes, high skills, and customization. Mass production uses high volumes, standardization, and low unit costs. Lean production reduces waste and improves quality and flow.
distractors: Craft production is high-volume and standardized, mass production is low-volume and customized, and lean production builds inventory.
Craft, mass, and lean production all use identical volumes and skill levels.
Lean production increases waste instead of improving quality, while mass production handcrafts every item to a unique design.

ch1-q11.answer: Teamwork, multiple skills, responsibility for improvement, and continual performance demands can place a heavy burden on employees.
distractors: Lean removes all employee responsibility because employees never participate in improvement.
Lean prohibits teamwork and multiple skills and requires no skills at all.
Lean has no performance or quality expectations, so employees need not engage in their work.

ch1-q12.answer: Matching demand and supply prevents excess inventory and shortages. Supply chain management coordinates quality, cost, and delivery from procurement to the customer.
distractors: Demand and supply should be set independently, and supply chain management should exclude the final customer.
Always producing more than demand eliminates both shortages and excess inventory.
Supply chain management coordinates advertising only, not costs or delivery.

ch1-q13.answer: The four sources are variety in goods or services, structural variation, random variation, and controllable variation.
distractors: All variation is random; structural and controllable variation do not exist.
Variety in goods and services is unrelated to variation, which comes only from equipment failures.
Only structural variation exists, so managers need not address anything beyond seasonality.

ch1-q14.answer: Possible reasons include personal gain, pressure to meet targets, organizational culture, a lack of ethical standards, and underestimating consequences.
distractors: Unethical behavior always results only from a lack of knowledge; culture and pressure have no influence.
Personal gain and pressure to meet targets do not affect ethical judgment.
Underestimating consequences always guarantees ethical behavior.

ch1-q15.answer: Value added is created by transforming inputs into goods or services that are more valuable to customers.
distractors: Value added arises simply from increasing input costs and is unrelated to customer value.
Value added refers only to the value lost when finished products are discarded without processing.
Value added means the total amount a company has borrowed.

ch1-q16.answer: Outsourcing can provide specialist capabilities and reduce costs, but can make quality and delivery harder to control, affect employment, and create supply risks.
distractors: Outsourcing eliminates all quality, delivery, and supply risks.
Outsourcing never provides specialist capabilities and always increases costs.
Outsourcing affects advertising only and has no effect on employment or supply.

ch1-q17.answer: Sustainability means using resources without damaging the ecosystems that support future generations. It concerns design, procurement, disposal, and other activities.
distractors: Sustainability means maximizing current-period profit without considering resources for future generations.
Sustainability concerns disposal only and has no connection to design or procurement.
Sustainability means increasing resource consumption without limits.

ch2-q1.answer: Import restrictions may protect domestic industries and jobs, but can raise prices, reduce choice, and provoke retaliation.
distractors: Import restrictions always lower prices, increase choice, and cause no retaliation.
Import restrictions have no effect on domestic industries or employment.
Higher tariffs always benefit consumers and trading partners without any drawbacks.

ch2-q2.answer: Organizations compete through price, quality, differentiation, flexibility, delivery speed, service, location, and similar factors.
distractors: Organizations compete only through price; quality and delivery are not competitive factors.
Quality, service, and location do not affect competition; advertising volume alone matters.
Organizations must avoid flexibility and differentiation when competing.

ch2-q3.answer: Order qualifiers are minimum requirements for consideration; order winners are the factors that actually determine the choice.
distractors: Order qualifiers determine the final purchase, while order winners are the minimum requirements for consideration.
Order qualifiers and order winners have the same meaning and need not be distinguished.
Order qualifiers measure post-purchase satisfaction, while order winners mean accounting profit only.

ch2-q4.answer: For example, convenience stores compete on location and convenience, while discount stores compete on low prices and product assortment.
distractors: Convenience stores do not use location or convenience, and discount stores do not use prices to compete.
Since stores have the same customers, they must all use exactly one competitive approach.
All stores compete through high prices alone.

ch2-q5.answer: The Balanced Scorecard evaluates strategy from perspectives such as finance, customers, internal processes, and learning and growth.
distractors: The Balanced Scorecard evaluates financial profit only and excludes customers and learning.
The Balanced Scorecard is only a daily count of inventory.
The Balanced Scorecard evaluates employee working hours only.

ch2-q6.answer: Strategy sets the long-term direction; tactics are specific actions used to implement it.
distractors: Strategy consists of daily tasks, while tactics set the long-term direction.
Strategy and tactics are unrelated, and tactics do not support strategy.
Both strategy and tactics are merely measures that record past performance.

ch2-q7.answer: Organization strategy sets company-wide goals; operations strategy sets the production and service policies that help achieve them.
distractors: Organization strategy concerns only production policies, while operations strategy sets company-wide goals.
Operations strategy is independent of organization strategy and need not support company-wide goals.
Both organization strategy and operations strategy refer only to equipment repair schedules.

ch2-q8.answer: Time-based strategies compete by reducing development time, order-processing time, delivery time, and similar lead times.
distractors: Time-based strategies deliberately lengthen delivery, development, and order-processing times.
Time-based strategies lower prices only and do not consider time.
Time-based strategies mean only keeping production volume constant regardless of time.

ch2-q9.answer: Productivity is output divided by input. It supports comparisons over time and across departments and affects competitiveness. Operations is mainly responsible; efficiency describes how little resource use is wasted.
distractors: Productivity is input divided by output, so increasing inputs with unchanged output improves productivity.
Productivity measures total sales only, without considering inputs or departmental comparisons.
Productivity and efficiency are always identical, and neither concerns resource inputs.

ch2-q10.answer: Technology, skills, equipment, quality, work methods, management, and materials affect productivity. Training, automation, standardization, and reducing defects can improve it.
distractors: Only the number of workers determines productivity; technology, quality, and equipment have no effect.
Increasing defects and reducing training always improve productivity.
Standardization and better work methods have no effect on productivity.

ch2-q11.answer: Differences in automation, process design, quality management, standardization, training, and equipment investment may explain differences in labor productivity.
distractors: Labor productivity differences depend only on how hard workers work, not on process design.
Automation, training, and quality management should be excluded when comparing labor productivity.
Labor productivity must be identical even when equipment investment differs.

ch2-q12.answer: Midsize aircraft on direct routes offer flexibility and convenience; large aircraft operating through hubs offer economies of scale in mass transport.
distractors: Midsize direct flights always provide the greatest mass-transport economies, while large hub flights offer only route flexibility.
The two strategies have no differences in convenience or transport scale.
Large-aircraft hub operations do not require any concentration of demand.

ch2-q13.answer: Banks can compete through interest rates, fees, ATMs, location, opening hours, apps, online transactions, customer service, product range, and reliability.
distractors: Banks compete only on interest rates; fees and apps do not affect customer acquisition.
Reducing reliability and customer service attracts customers at every bank.
Opening hours, location, and ATMs have no effect on customers choosing a bank.

ch2-q14.answer: Reducing processing variation makes processes easier to standardize, mechanize, and automate.
distractors: Increasing processing variation always makes automation with the same procedures easier.
Standardization obstructs mechanization, so common process steps should be avoided.
Variation has no relationship to the use of technology.

ch2-q15.answer: The material gives FedEx and Zara as time-based examples, and Lexus and Rolex as quality-based examples.
distractors: The material gives Lexus and Rolex as time-based examples, and FedEx and Zara as quality-based examples.
The material presents FedEx and Zara as companies that do not emphasize speed or delivery.
The material presents Lexus and Rolex as companies that do not compete on quality.

ch3-q1.answer: Quantitative forecasts offer objectivity, reproducibility, and large-scale data processing, but struggle with insufficient historical data, structural change, and factors that cannot be quantified.
distractors: Quantitative forecasts are always accurate despite structural change and do not need historical data.
Quantitative forecasts lack objectivity and reproducibility and cannot process numerical data.
Quantitative forecasts always capture every factor that cannot be quantified.

ch3-q2.answer: Inaccurate forecasts can cause shortages, excess inventory, too few or too many staff or facilities, higher costs, and lower customer satisfaction.
distractors: Inaccurate forecasts have no effect on inventory, staffing, or customer satisfaction.
Larger forecast errors always reduce costs and shortages.
Forecast errors affect only selling prices and cannot cause excess or insufficient capacity.

ch3-q3.answer: Consumer surveys may differ from actual behavior; salesforce estimates may have optimistic or pessimistic bias; executive committees may suffer from groupthink and insufficient frontline information.
distractors: Consumer responses always match behavior, and salesforce estimates have no bias.
Executive committees never experience groupthink and always have sufficient frontline information.
Consumer surveys, salesforce estimates, and executive opinions are all free from bias.

ch3-q4.answer: The future is uncertain, so forecasts do not exactly match actual results. Even a good forecast retains small random errors.
distractors: A good forecast always matches actual results exactly.
A forecast can be wrong only because of a calculation mistake; uncertainty does not exist.
Random errors can always be completely eliminated regardless of the amount of data.

ch3-q5.answer: Control limits monitor whether forecast errors exceed their normal range, helping detect model problems or changes.
distractors: Control limits are set to guarantee zero forecast error.
Control limits make checking errors unnecessary by ensuring abnormalities are missed.
Control limits allow forecast values to be treated as actual sales.

ch3-q6.answer: Consider demand variation, the cost of errors, the required sensitivity, and tolerance for false alarms.
distractors: Always use the narrowest possible limits and ignore the cost of false alarms.
Always use the widest possible limits and ignore sensitivity to abnormalities.
Demand variation and the cost of errors are irrelevant when setting control limits.

ch3-q7.answer: MAD averages absolute errors and is easy to interpret. MSE squares errors and penalizes large deviations more heavily.
distractors: MAD averages squared errors, while MSE averages absolute errors.
Both MAD and MSE simply average signed errors without changing them.
MSE is used to penalize large deviations less heavily than MAD.

ch3-q8.answer: Exponential smoothing can be updated using only the latest forecast and actual value, requiring little stored data and simple calculations.
distractors: Exponential smoothing requires storing all past observations again before every update.
Exponential smoothing ignores actual values and always repeats only the previous forecast.
Exponential smoothing always needs more stored data than a moving average.

ch3-q9.answer: Fewer periods make a moving average more responsive; more periods produce smoother forecasts but slower responses to change.
distractors: More periods make a moving average more responsive, while fewer periods slow its response.
Changing the number of periods has no effect on responsiveness.
Adding more periods always reduces the smoothing effect.

ch3-q10.answer: A larger alpha gives more weight to the latest actual value and responds faster; a smaller alpha is smoother and more stable. Choose it considering demand variation and errors.
distractors: A larger alpha reduces the influence of the latest actual value and slows the response.
Alpha should be chosen without considering demand variation or forecast errors.
A smaller alpha makes the forecast respond only to the latest actual value.

ch3-q11.answer: Collect local five-day forecasts and observed results, then compare errors in temperature, precipitation, and other measures.
distractors: Judge forecast accuracy from its appearance without collecting actual observations.
Establish accuracy by comparing forecasts with observations from a different place and time.
Treat forecast values as actual results to verify accuracy.

ch3-q12.answer: A centered moving average covering one full seasonal cycle averages out seasonal ups and downs within the cycle.
distractors: Averaging over a full seasonal cycle always amplifies seasonal ups and downs.
A centered moving average removes seasonality because it uses only one point in the cycle.
Seasonal length is irrelevant; every number of periods has exactly the same effect.

ch3-q13.answer: Demand is the quantity customers want; sales are the quantity actually sold.
distractors: Demand is the quantity actually sold; sales are the quantity customers would like to buy if stock were available.
Sales and demand are always equal, even during stockouts.
Demand means production capacity, while sales mean the quality customers want.

ch3-q14.answer: A reactive approach forecasts demand and responds to it; a proactive approach influences demand through advertising, prices, and promotions.
distractors: A reactive approach changes demand through advertising; a proactive approach only adjusts supply to a forecast.
Both reactive and proactive approaches observe demand without taking action.
A proactive approach cannot influence demand through prices or promotions.

ch3-q15.answer: Greater process flexibility makes it easier to respond to forecast errors later. Longer forecast horizons increase uncertainty.
distractors: Greater flexibility makes forecast errors harder to address, and longer horizons reduce uncertainty.
Flexibility guarantees perfectly accurate forecasts over every horizon.
Forecast horizon, uncertainty, and process flexibility have no relationship.

ch3-q16.answer: Supply chain forecasting requires information sharing and coordination across firms. It can reduce inventory, shortages, and variation, but faces delays, inconsistent information, and confidentiality concerns.
distractors: Supply chain forecasting does not require information sharing or coordination across firms.
Supply chain forecasting never faces information delays or confidentiality concerns.
Forecasting for an entire supply chain can always be completed using only one company's internal forecast.

ch3-q17.answer: Neither is universally superior. Quantitative methods suit abundant data; qualitative methods are useful for new products and situations with little precedent.
distractors: Quantitative methods are always superior, and historical data are unnecessary even for new products.
Qualitative methods are always superior, and abundant numerical data have no value.
Both methods always achieve the same accuracy regardless of the situation.

ch3-q18.answer: Useful information includes previous-version sales, preorders, the customer base, prices, promotions, competitors, launch timing, compatibility, and reviews.
distractors: Previous-version sales alone are sufficient; prices, competitors, and compatibility should be ignored.
Only price determines demand for a new version; preorders and the customer base are unnecessary.
Reviews, promotions, and launch timing have no relevance to demand forecasting.

ch3-q19.answer: Use seasonality for Mother's Day cards, surveys for a new Netflix release, Delphi for moon travel, associative or causal methods for a marmalade price increase, and averaging or naive methods for supermarket toothpaste.
distractors: Ignore seasonality for Mother's Day cards, use only past sales of the same unreleased Netflix title, and use a simple moving average for moon travel.
Ignore the price-demand relationship for a marmalade price increase, and forecast moon travel only from abundant historical sales.
Exclude seasonality, surveys, and expert opinion for every item, and use the same simple average for all of them.

ch4-q1.answer: Reasons include changing customer needs, competition, technological innovation, regulation, cost or quality problems, and environmental requirements.
distractors: Redesign concerns appearance only and is unrelated to customer needs or regulation.
Technological innovation and quality problems cannot be reasons to redesign.
Once designed, a product or service should never be redesigned even when competition changes.

ch4-q2.answer: Basic research seeks principles and new knowledge; applied research seeks to use knowledge to solve specific problems.
distractors: Basic research focuses only on specific applications, while applied research focuses only on discovering principles.
Basic and applied research have identical purposes and need not be distinguished.
Neither basic nor applied research concerns knowledge or problem-solving.

ch4-q3.answer: CAD means computer-aided design. Designers use it for drawings, 3D models, modifications, simulations, and sharing designs.
distractors: CAD only forecasts finished-product sales and cannot be used for drawings.
CAD means hand-drawn plans that do not use computers.
CAD only manages inventory and cannot modify or share designs.

ch4-q4.answer: Standardization can reduce costs, provide interchangeability, and make quality more consistent, but can reduce choice and make customization harder.
distractors: Standardization always provides unlimited choices and reduces interchangeability.
Higher costs are a benefit of standardization, while consistent quality is a drawback.
Standardization never makes customization harder and has no drawbacks.

ch4-q5.answer: Modular design combines independent components or units. It simplifies replacement, repair, and combinations, but can impose design constraints.
distractors: Modular design makes the whole product inseparable and harder to replace or repair.
Modular design uses no independent units and requires building everything from scratch each time.
Modular design has no constraints, and any components can be combined without conditions.

ch4-q6.answer: Design for manufacturing considers ease of production. Reducing parts, process steps, and assembly effort can improve quality and costs.
distractors: Design for manufacturing ignores production needs and increases parts and assembly effort.
Design for manufacturing concerns advertising only, not quality or costs.
Design for manufacturing postpones manufacturability until design is complete and ignores processes.

ch4-q7.answer: Concurrent engineering involves early, simultaneous cooperation among design, manufacturing, procurement, and other functions. It shortens development time, reduces rework, and improves quality.
distractors: Concurrent engineering means departments work sequentially without sharing information with the next department.
Concurrent engineering prohibits manufacturing and procurement from participating until design is finished.
Concurrent engineering reduces rework by avoiding early cooperation.

ch4-q8.answer: Remanufacturing disassembles, inspects, and restores used products to make them usable again.
distractors: Remanufacturing sells used products as new without inspection.
Remanufacturing means only melting products down into raw materials.
Remanufacturing assembles new products only and never uses used products.

ch4-q9.answer: A life cycle runs from introduction through growth and maturity to decline. Design should consider demand, maintenance, and disposal. New uses include deodorizing, cleaning, and cooking for baking soda; repairs, fastening, and crafts for duct tape; and cooking, cleaning, and deodorizing for vinegar.
distractors: A life cycle covers manufacturing time only, so maintenance and disposal are irrelevant.
Every product grows forever after introduction, so new uses and decline need not be considered.
Baking soda, duct tape, and vinegar have no uses beyond their original applications.

ch4-q10.answer: R&D produces new technologies, materials, processes, and quality improvements, making higher output possible from the same inputs.
distractors: R&D only increases inputs and cannot improve technology, processes, or quality.
R&D concerns appearance only and has no connection to productivity.
Improving productivity requires stopping R&D and avoiding new materials and processes.

ch4-q11.answer: Mass customization combines the efficiency of mass production with the ability to meet individual orders.
distractors: Mass customization supplies exactly the same specification to every customer.
Mass customization means completely abandoning the efficiency of mass production.
Mass customization rejects individual orders and sells only stocked products.

ch4-q12.answer: Services involve greater customer contact, and their production and consumption often occur simultaneously.
distractors: Services have no customer contact, and production and consumption always occur at separate times.
Services are all tangible and can always be supplied from finished-goods inventory.
Service design need not consider customer participation or the time of delivery.

ch4-q13.answer: Robust design keeps performance stable despite variation in operating conditions or processes.
distractors: Robust design deliberately makes performance vary greatly with the environment.
Robust design means only keeping all operating conditions permanently ideal.
Robust design ignores variation in processes.

ch4-q14.answer: Quality function deployment systematically translates the voice of the customer into design and technical specifications.
distractors: QFD excludes customer input and bases specifications only on engineers' preferences.
QFD only totals finished-product sales and is not used in design.
QFD fixes specifications independently of customer requirements.

ch4-q15.answer: Reverse engineering analyzes existing products to understand their structure and operation. Its ethical acceptability depends on intellectual property rights and how the results are used.
distractors: Reverse engineering is always legal and ethical regardless of how it is used.
Reverse engineering excludes analysis of existing products and means only designing from scratch.
Reverse engineering does not require considering intellectual property rights.

ch4-q16.answer: Value analysis removes unnecessary costs while maintaining function.
distractors: Value analysis minimizes costs even if necessary functions are lost.
Value analysis increases unnecessary costs to raise selling prices.
Value analysis does not examine the relationship between function and cost.

ch4-q17.answer: Life cycle assessment evaluates environmental impacts from raw-material extraction through manufacturing, use, and disposal.
distractors: LCA evaluates factory electricity only and excludes raw materials, use, and disposal.
LCA sets selling prices and does not concern environmental impacts.
LCA evaluates disposal only and ignores the overall product life cycle.

ch4-q18.answer: The three Rs are Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle.
distractors: The three Rs mean increased production, higher prices, and mass disposal.
The three Rs mean only Reduce, Replace, and Reject, excluding reuse.
The three Rs encourage greater resource consumption and disposal.

ch4-q19.answer: For example, smartphone facial recognition was once a surprising feature and is now common. On-device AI is a possible future standard. Contactless payment has become common in services, while advanced personalization is another possible future standard.
distractors: Delight features never become standard features over time.
The material says facial recognition and contactless payment do not exist today.
The material guarantees that on-device AI and advanced personalization will become standard in every industry.

ch5-q1.answer: Design capacity is maximum capacity under ideal conditions. Effective capacity is achievable capacity after considering actual constraints.
distractors: Design capacity considers actual constraints, while effective capacity is the ideal maximum.
Both design and effective capacity mean the quantity actually sold.
Effective capacity ignores constraints such as breakdowns and setups.

ch5-q2.answer: Equipment failures, staff shortages, quality defects, and setup time can prevent full use of capacity.
distractors: Capacity utilization always remains unchanged despite equipment failures or staff shortages.
Only selling prices prevent capacity use; quality and setups have no effect.
Quality defects and setup time always increase capacity utilization.

ch5-q3.answer: Long-term planning concerns major investments such as equipment and location. Short-term planning adjusts shifts, overtime, inventory, and similar factors.
distractors: Long-term planning concerns only today's overtime; short-term planning concerns only building new factories.
Both long-term and short-term capacity planning mean changing major investments immediately.
Short-term capacity adjustments cannot use shifts or overtime.

ch5-q4.answer: Annual examples include heaters and ski resorts; monthly examples include seasonal-event products and month-end accounting services; weekly examples include food and weekend restaurants; daily examples include newspapers and commuter transport.
distractors: Heaters and ski resorts have no annual seasonal patterns.
Demand for commuter transport never changes by time of day and has no daily pattern.
Goods and services have no annual, monthly, weekly, or daily demand variation.

ch5-q5.answer: Use cross-training, reserve equipment, modularity, room for expansion, flexible working arrangements, and outsourcing.
distractors: Increase flexibility by restricting workers to one skill, removing expansion space, and prohibiting outsourcing.
Dedicated equipment and completely fixed work schedules make a system more flexible.
Reserve equipment and modularity have no connection to flexibility.

ch5-q6.answer: Expanding one process does not increase total output if another process remains the bottleneck.
distractors: Increasing one process's capacity always increases total output regardless of other processes.
Bottlenecks have no effect on total system output.
Capacity plans become more accurate when links between departments are ignored.

ch5-q7.answer: Capacity is added in discrete units, such as one machine or one classroom, rather than as a continuous quantity.
distractors: All equipment capacity can be increased continuously by any fractional amount.
Capacity in chunks means only dividing customers' demand into smaller portions.
Adding machines or classrooms in whole units has no implications for investment or unused capacity.

ch5-q8.answer: Changing enrollment can cause shortages or surpluses of classrooms and teachers. Responses include expansion, district adjustments, temporary classrooms, and changes in class organization.
distractors: Changes in enrollment do not affect the required number of classrooms or teachers.
District adjustments and temporary classrooms cannot address classroom shortages.
Continuously adding classrooms always solves capacity problems regardless of enrollment.

ch5-q9.answer: A systems approach plans the capacity of related processes and departments together to identify bottlenecks and wider effects.
distractors: A systems approach separates departments and optimizes each process independently.
A systems approach ignores bottlenecks and considers only selected equipment.
A systems approach does not examine effects on other departments.

ch5-q10.answer: Too little capacity can cause lost opportunities and congestion. Too much capacity increases equipment-cost burdens and can lower productivity.
distractors: More capacity always produces higher productivity.
Too little capacity cannot cause congestion or lost opportunities.
Equipment costs and capacity shortages or surpluses have no connection to productivity.

ch5-q11.answer: A mismatch between product requirements and process capability can cause quality problems, higher costs, and late delivery.
distractors: A mismatch between product requirements and process capability has no effect on quality, costs, or delivery.
The less a process meets product requirements, the better the quality always becomes.
Product requirements should be set only through advertising, without checking process capability.

ch5-q12.answer: Uncertainty in demand, technology, and costs calls for considering phased expansion, capacity cushions, and flexible alternatives.
distractors: Under uncertainty, making the largest possible investment all at once is always optimal.
Uncertainty has no effect on capacity decisions, so demand forecasts are unnecessary.
Uncertain demand and technology are reasons to avoid flexibility and capacity cushions.

ch5-q13.answer: Police and fire staffing must consider emergency peaks and response times, not just average demand.
distractors: Average demand alone always guarantees an adequate emergency response.
Police and fire planning should ignore response times and the risk of simultaneous incidents.
Peak demand exists only in routine business and never in emergency services.

ch5-q14.answer: Capacity has long-term effects on investment costs, revenue opportunities, customer satisfaction, and future flexibility.
distractors: Capacity planning concerns today's shifts only and has no connection to long-term investments.
Capacity shortages and surpluses do not affect revenue opportunities or customer satisfaction.
Factory and store size can be changed instantly at no cost, making capacity decisions unimportant.

ch5-q15.answer: Services are hard to store and are strongly affected by demand variation, customer participation, and time and location constraints.
distractors: Services are easy to store, so customer location and timing can be ignored.
Services have no demand variation, so their capacity planning is always easier than for goods.
Unused service appointments can always be carried forward as finished-goods inventory.

ch5-q16.answer: A university can use student intake; a hospital, bed count; a computer repair shop, repairs per day; and a farm, annual harvest.
distractors: A university uses units sold; a hospital, crop yields; a repair shop, bed count; and a farm, student numbers.
Every facility must use exactly the same capacity unit without specifying a time period.
Universities and hospitals cannot use throughput or intake as capacity measures.

ch5-q17.answer: Quantifying capacity allows comparison with demand, expansion decisions, utilization calculations, and bottleneck identification.
distractors: Capacity measures always equal actual sales and are not used for comparison with demand.
Quantifying capacity makes it impossible to identify bottlenecks or expansion needs.
Capacity measures serve advertising only and cannot support utilization calculations or decisions.
